findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 17032026 1900 Pensions Committee and Board
findings.headline: Pension fund investment performance noted as relatively strong for quarter ended 31 December 2025

Some managers underperformed, particularly Blackrock, but positive recovery was noted from Ruffer due to equity allocation and gold investment. European and UK equities performed well, with inflation coming back under control.
findings.matters: Better investment returns support long-term fund sustainability and reduce future contribution burdens on the council and other employers in the fund.
findings.figures: Quarter ended 31 December 2025; detailed figures in exempt reports
findings.quote: It was explained what the current investment portfolio was, and what the returns were. It was additionally explained what the performance of the fund was and noted that it was currently performing relatively strongly. Steve Turner, Mercer explained that that the fund was performing generally well.

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 17032026 1900 Pensions Committee and Board
findings.headline: Cyber-attack affecting three Triborough councils triggered temporary communications quarantine at Haringey Pension Fund
findings.detail: A cyber-attack affected Royal Borough of Kensington & Chelsea, Hammersmith and Fulham, and Westminster, prompting Haringey Pension Fund to quarantine communications from those councils to prevent infection. The fund confirmed all data is encrypted and backups held offsite. Officers will monitor any impact and implement lessons learned.
findings.matters: Demonstrates operational IT security risks in the local government system; Haringey's response protocol shows incident preparedness but highlights ongoing vulnerability in interconnected council systems.
findings.figures: Three councils affected
findings.quote: It was explained that there had been a recent of cyber-attack in the Triborough (RBKC, Hammersmith and Fulham and Westminster), which facilitated the fund's response to quarantine communication from those boroughs temporarily to prevent infection. It was noted that all data was encrypted and backups held offsite to ensure security.

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 17032026 1900 Pensions Committee and Board
findings.headline: Pension fund implements first formal business plan and budget; expected to become statutory requirement
findings.detail: The committee approved the pension fund's first formal business plan and budget for 2026/27, implementing governance review recommendations. The fund expects this will become a statutory requirement. The plan spans three years with most milestones in the first year; quarterly monitoring reports will be provided to the committee.
findings.matters: Formalization of pension fund planning reflects governance best practice but may signal increasing administrative and compliance costs for the council.
findings.figures: Three-year plan; quarterly monitoring
findings.quote: It was explained that this was the Pension Fund's first formal Business Plan and Budget, which was within the recommendations of the governance review, as well as an expectation that this will become a statutory requirement.

findings.paper_title: Printed minutes 17032026 1900 Pensions Committee and Board
findings.headline: Pension fund secondary contribution rate set at 2.8% for next three years
findings.detail: The triennial actuarial valuation sets the employer secondary contribution rate at 2.8% for the whole fund for the next three years. Haringey Council comprises the majority of the fund and acts as a stabilising employer. This rate-setting approach is common across other Local Government Pension Funds.
findings.matters: The secondary rate directly affects the council's budget requirements for pension contributions and signals the fund's funding position; a stable rate indicates the fund is in reasonable health relative to liabilities.
findings.quote: It was noted that the contributions to the secondary rate was set at 2.8% for the next few years for the whole Fund, and that Haringey Council made up the majority of the fund, which made them a stabilising employer.

findings.headline: Actual inflation in April 2026 of 3.8% exceeded the 3.3% assumption in the March 2025 valuation
findings.detail: Observed inflation has been higher than anticipated, resulting in LGPS pension increases of 3.8% in April 2026 against the 3.3% assumption embedded in the 2025 valuation. This increases the present value of promised pension liabilities. The actuary notes this inflation trajectory requires monitoring for assumption revisions.
findings.matters: Higher inflation drives up the cost of pension benefits and creates upward pressure on funding position; indicates that assumption revisions may be required at the next valuation in 2028
findings.figures: Actual benefit inflation April 2026: 3.8%; 2025 valuation assumption: 3.3%; variance: +50 basis points
findings.quote: Observed inflation has been higher than anticipated over 2026, resulting in LGPS benefit increases of 3.8% in April 2026 and an increase in the value placed on the Fund's liabilities.

findings.headline: 79% of fund assets transitioned to London CIV pooling arrangement, below the March 2026 government target for full transfer
findings.detail: £1.671bn of £2.111bn net assets (79%) had transferred to the London Collective Investment Vehicle by year-end. Government 'Fit for the Future' guidance (May 2025) set expectation of 'transferring all assets by March 2026'. Asset pooling generated net savings of £1.288m to the fund in 2025/26 after accounting for all LCIV charges.
findings.matters: Incomplete asset pooling creates regulatory compliance uncertainty, though partially offset by demonstrated cost savings of £1.3m annually from pooling activity
findings.figures: Assets in LCIV: £1.671bn of £2.111bn (79%); net savings 2025/26: £1.288m after LCIV charges
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the Fund had transitioned £1.671 billion, representing 79% of its assets, into LCIV. In 2025/26, the net saving to the Fund for the year was £1.288million.

findings.headline: Administration costs per member rose 6.7% to £53.80, with staffing headcount up and vacancy rate at 23%
findings.detail: Cost per member increased from £50.41 to £53.80. Full-time equivalent staff expanded from 11.6 to 13.0. Vacancy rate across all administration staff stands at 23%. The 2025/26 year included one-off charges for software implementation and triennial actuarial valuation.
findings.matters: Rising per-member costs combined with elevated vacancy rate signal labour market pressures and capacity constraints that could affect administration service quality
findings.quote: Administration costs per member £53.80; Administration FTEs 13.0; Staff vacancy rate as % 23

findings.headline: Pension benefits paid exceeded contributions received by £6.7m, a structural position reflecting fund maturity
findings.detail: Benefits of £74.5m paid in 2025/26 exceeded contributions of £67.8m by £6.7m. This gap, covered by investment income in the year, reflects declining active membership relative to pensioners and deferred members. Benefits have exceeded contributions for several years.
findings.matters: Structural maturity makes the fund increasingly dependent on investment returns to fund benefit payments, reducing tolerance for sustained underperformance
findings.figures: Benefits paid £74.5m; contributions £67.8m; shortfall £6.7m
findings.quote: Contributions have grown at a slower pace than benefits paid, reflecting the increasing maturity of the Fund's membership profile. Benefits have exceeded contributions for several years, with the shortfall covered by investment income.

findings.headline: Fund valued at 139% of liabilities at 31 March 2025, with actuarial statement indicating likely strengthening since
findings.detail: Assets of £1,933m at the most recent actuarial valuation were valued at 139% of pension liabilities. The fund actuary stated: 'Overall, we estimate that the funding position is likely to be stronger than at the previous formal valuation at 31 March 2025.' Employer contribution rates are locked in through March 2029. Next valuation is at 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: Strong funding position removes solvency risk, confirms scheme sustainability, and protects participating employers from unexpected contribution rises
findings.figures: Assets £1,933m at 31 March 2025; funding level 139% of liabilities
findings.quote: The fund's assets, which at 31 March 2025 were valued at £1,933 million, were sufficient to meet 139% of the liabilities (i.e. the present value of promised retirement benefits) accrued up to that date.

findings.headline: Fund investment returns underperformed benchmarks across all time periods in 2025/26
findings.detail: One-year returns of 9.5% fell 90 basis points short of the 10.4% benchmark. Three-year returns of 7.7% trailed the 9.4% benchmark by 170bp. Five-year returns of 5.7% lagged the 6.8% benchmark by 110bp. The actuarial statement attributes recent volatility to US tariff increases and Middle East conflict.
findings.matters: Persistent underperformance against benchmarks is material to long-term fund sustainability, especially given the fund's mature membership profile where benefits increasingly exceed contributions
findings.figures: 1 year: 9.5% actual vs 10.4% benchmark; 3 year: 7.7% vs 9.4%; 5 year: 5.7% vs 6.8%
findings.quote: 1 year 10.4% benchmark 9.5% actual; 3 year 9.4% benchmark 7.7% actual; 5 year 6.8% benchmark 5.7% actual

findings.headline: No significant control deficiencies identified; one other control deficiency remains (journal posting)
findings.detail: The audit has identified zero significant control deficiencies in the pension fund's control environment. The only control deficiency reported is the segregation of duties issue on journal posting, classified as an 'other control deficiency' rather than significant in audit terms. No significant control deficiencies existed in the prior year.
findings.matters: The absence of significant control deficiencies provides positive assurance on the design and operating effectiveness of the fund's key internal controls, though the continuing journal posting weakness limits the overall control environment assessment.
findings.figures: 0 significant control deficiencies; 1 other control deficiency; 0 prior-year deficiencies remediated
findings.quote: These are significant control deficiencies which increase the likelihood and potential magnitude of a material misstatement in the financial statements. We have identified no significant control deficiencies in the current year.

findings.headline: Unmodified audit opinion expected; no reportable misstatements or fraud indicators identified
findings.detail: KPMG expects to issue an unmodified auditor's report on the pension fund's financial statements for the year to 31 March 2026. During audit procedures, including testing of management override of controls and high-risk journals using KPMG Clara analysis, no reportable misstatements or indicators of fraud were identified. No suspected or alleged incidents of management override were found.
findings.matters: A clean audit opinion with no fraud findings provides assurance on the integrity of the financial statements and management control environment, particularly important given investments represent 99.89% of the fund's material assets.
findings.figures: No reportable misstatements; no fraud indicators identified
findings.quote: We found no reportable misstatements or indicators of fraud in our testing. We expect to issue an unmodified Auditor's Report

findings.headline: £5.96m adjustment made to investment valuations; updated valuations not available at year-end closedown
findings.detail: The auditors identified and management corrected a misstatement of £5.96m relating to Level 3 investments (unquoted and illiquid assets where valuations depend on fund managers' information). Updated valuations were not available when the pension fund closed its accounts on 31 March 2026 and were only received from fund managers after year-end. The audit adjustment updated the investment balance to reflect these subsequent valuations. Level 3 investments are a significant portion of the fund's holdings.
findings.matters: A material post-year-end adjustment to investment valuations indicates the pension fund's year-end financial position was incomplete and that its valuation processes for complex illiquid assets do not conclude by the accounting close date.
findings.figures: £5.96m adjustment; investments represent 99.89% of total pension fund assets
findings.quote: Due to the timing of the funds' valuation processes, updated valuations were not available at the Fund's year-end closedown. The audit adjustment updates the investment balance to reflect the subsequent valuations received from the fund managers after the year end.

findings.headline: Segregation of duties control deficiency on manual journal posting recurs from prior year; auditors cannot rely on management's informal compensating control
findings.detail: The audit identifies that there are no segregation of duties controls when posting manual journals directly to the ledger, and journals below £40,000 do not require approval by another person. This deficiency was also raised in the prior year and remains unresolved. Management implemented a compensating control to review journals impacting balance sheet movements, but auditors cannot rely on this as it remains informal in nature and lacks formal status. Management acknowledges the issue and commits to implement a 'park and post' approach for all journals by April 2027.
findings.matters: A recurring control weakness over journal posting creates fraud risk and financial statement accuracy risk; the informality of compensating controls means the underlying deficiency remains unmitigated despite prior-year notification.
findings.figures: Journals below £40,000 exempt from approval requirement; implementation deadline April 2027
findings.quote: We identified that there are no segregation of duties controls when posting manual journals directly to the ledger. We identified that management have implemented a compensating control to review any manual journals which impact balance sheet movements, however for the purposes of our audit, we are unable to rely on this control as it is informal in nature

findings.headline: All employer and employee contributions accounted for and remitted on schedule for the quarter to 30 June 2026.
findings.detail: The paper confirms that 'all expected payments and corresponding contribution schedules are accounted for as at the publication date of this report.' Both employer and employee contributions are being collected and remitted within expected timeframes, indicating fund revenue streams are operating within normal parameters.
findings.matters: Contribution collection is fundamental to pension fund solvency and council financial health; on-schedule collection indicates the fund's cash position is being managed within target and the council is meeting its employer contribution obligations.
findings.figures: Not specified in report.
findings.quote: Officers confirm that all expected payments and corresponding contribution schedules are accounted for as at the publication date of this report.

findings.headline: Transfer case processing fell below 20-day service level agreement targets following departure of experienced transfer specialist.
findings.detail: Transfer cases (both inbound and outbound, quotations and actuals) are performing below their service level targets. Transfer-in actuals completed at 71% within the 20-day SLA (7 cases); transfer-out actuals at 72% within target (86 cases). The paper attributes this to 'resourcing challenges arising from the departure of an experienced transfer specialist and the associated knowledge gap within the team.' Recruitment and training are underway, with performance expected to improve over the course of the year.
findings.matters: Finance directors track staffing retention and operational resilience in critical pension administration; peer councils recognise specialist staffing loss as a shared pressure; lenders assess service delivery risk and administrative capacity.
findings.figures: Transfer in actual: 71% within 20-day SLA (7 cases). Transfer out actual: 72% within 20-day SLA (86 cases).
findings.quote: However, performance for transfer cases, including both transfers in and transfers out, across both quotations and actuals, are below target. This reflects resourcing challenges arising from the departure of an experienced transfer specialist and the associated knowledge gap within the team.

findings.headline: Strategic Implementation Plan agreed to increase allocations to credit, private credit and UK government bonds using part of the fund's cash holdings to realign portfolio with strategic asset allocation targets
findings.detail: A rebalancing plan (reviewed August 2026, presented to Investment and Governance Working Group September 2026) was agreed to deploy part of the fund's cash holdings. The fund is currently overweight in cash (4.8% vs 0% target) and listed equity (44.3% vs 40% target), and underweight in property, credit, and private credit.
findings.matters: Portfolio rebalancing decisions affect future fund returns and risk exposure; the timing and execution of cash deployment can impact investment performance and the trajectory of employer contribution requirements
findings.figures: Cash 4.8% actual vs 0% target; Listed equity 44.3% vs 40% target; Private Credit 0.0% vs 2.5% target; Credit 15.2% vs 17.5% target; Property 13.0% vs 15.5% target
findings.quote: The agreed plan focuses on increasing allocations to credit, private credit and UK government bonds using part of the Fund's cash holdings. These actions are expected to bring the Fund's portfolio closer to its strategic targets whilst maintaining an appropriate balance between return generation, risk management and liquidity requirements.

findings.headline: Fund underperformed benchmark across all reporting periods: last quarter 6.1% vs 7.1%, one year 12.7% vs 14.4%, three years 9.7% vs 12.3%, five years 6.0% vs 7.7%
findings.detail: Despite positive absolute returns, the fund consistently underperformed its benchmark across every timeframe measured. Persistent underperformance across different time horizons suggests a sustained gap between fund performance and strategic expectations.
findings.matters: Sustained underperformance against benchmark may signal strategy mismatch or management issues; performance gaps of this scale can affect the fund's ability to achieve long-term targets and contribute to upward pressure on employer contribution rates
findings.figures: Last quarter 6.1% actual vs 7.1% benchmark; one year 12.7% vs 14.4%; three years 9.7% vs 12.3%; five years 6.0% vs 7.7%
findings.quote: Although the Fund underperformed its benchmark over these periods, returns remained positive and continue to support the Fund's long-term investment objective.

findings.headline: Haringey Pension Fund valued at £2.22bn as of 30 June 2026, up £124m from previous quarter, with positive 6.1% quarterly return
findings.detail: The fund has grown from £1.71bn in 2022/23 to £2.22bn by June 2026. The £124m quarterly increase was driven primarily by positive returns in listed equity and credit markets. Fund growth over the five-year period shows consistent asset accumulation.
findings.matters: Fund growth reduces pressure for employer contribution rate increases and supports the council's ability to maintain stable pension costs within its revenue budget
findings.figures: £2.22bn current valuation; £124m increase from prior quarter; 6.1% quarterly return; fund grown from £1.71bn in 2022/23 to £2.22bn by June 2026
findings.quote: As at 30 June 2026, the Fund was valued at approximately £2.22bn, an increase of £124m from the previous quarter. The increase was driven by primarily by positive investment returns across the listed equity and credit markets during the quarter.

findings.headline: Mandatory asset pooling regulations took effect 30 June 2026; Haringey's pension fund investment management transferred to London CIV under agreement signed April 2026
findings.detail: New LGPS regulations require all administering authorities to participate in an FCA-regulated asset pool company managing investment assets. Haringey signed its Investment Management Agreement with London CIV in April 2026, formally delegating asset management responsibilities while retaining responsibility for setting investment strategy and monitoring the pool's performance.
findings.matters: Governance and oversight changes affect the council's control of pension fund management and its ability to influence performance; pooled management affects how the council monitors investment strategy implementation and cost control
findings.figures: Regulations effective 30 June 2026; Investment Management Agreement signed April 2026
findings.quote: The Pension Schemes Act 2026 and the Local Government Pension Scheme (Pooling, Management and Investment of Funds) Regulations 2026 took effect on 30 June 2026, enforcing mandatory asset pooling and strengthening fund governance across local government pensions.

findings.headline: Audit fee for 2024/25 of £88,000 represents increase from previous years
findings.detail: The public sector audit fee for 2024/25 is £88,000, an increase from prior years. Fee is based on assumptions about timely completion of audit evidence and supporting schedules; deviations from assumptions, including changes to deadlines or reporting requirements, may result in further increases.
findings.matters: Audit fee trends show cost pressures in pension fund administration, relevant to councils monitoring governance costs and to lenders assessing council expenditure management
findings.quote: The proposed fees for the 202 4/25 audit are £88,000. This fee, an increase from previous years, is based on several assumptions such as the timely completion of audit evidence files and provision of supporting schedules.

findings.headline: Misstatement in Level 3 investment valuations identified and corrected after delayed receipt of year-end valuations from fund managers
findings.detail: A misstatement relating to Level 3 investments (unquoted and illiquid assets) was identified and corrected during audit. The error occurred because valuations from fund managers were not available at the Fund's year-end closedown and had to be updated after the standard close process.
findings.matters: Investment valuations are material to pension fund financial statements; timing delays in receiving end-of-year valuations suggest process issues that could affect accuracy and timeliness of financial reporting
findings.figures: One misstatement in Level 3 investments (corrected)
findings.quote: There has been an identified and corrected misstatement. This relates to Level 3 investments, which comprise unquoted and illiquid assets where valuations are based on information provided by the underlying fund managers. Due to the timing of the funds' valuation processes, updated valuations were not available at the Fund's year-end closedown.

findings.committee: Culture, Community Safety & Environment Scrutiny Panel
findings.paper_title: 202627 Finance Update Report Quarter 1, 01/10/2026 Adults & Health Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: External auditors issued statutory recommendation on savings delivery; council accepted 3-year Financial Resilience Plan and CIPFA review
findings.detail: External auditors issued statutory recommendation citing persistent failure to deliver savings targets and inadequate arrangements for identification and monitoring of savings schemes. Full Council accepted this recommendation on 20 July 2026. Council's response includes implementation of 3-year Financial Resilience Plan, continuation and enhancement of spend controls, and governance on capital and commissioning. Government has commissioned CIPFA to carry out Financial Resilience Review focusing on financial management and governance.
findings.matters: A statutory audit recommendation is a formal flag that the authority's arrangements are below legal standard. CIPFA review indicates government concern beyond normal monitoring. Both signal that lenders and peers are watching closely.
findings.figures: Statutory recommendation issued on savings delivery; Financial Resilience Plan implementation required; CIPFA review commissioned
findings.quote: Non-delivery of savings has been raised by the Council's external auditors in a statutory recommendation and the Council's response was agreed by Full Council on 20 July... As part of the agreement by Government of the Council's £84.3m EFS requirement, Ministry of Housing Communities and Local Government have commissioned CIPFA to carry out a Financial Resilience Review.

findings.committee: Culture, Community Safety & Environment Scrutiny Panel
findings.paper_title: 202627 Finance Update Report Quarter 1, 01/10/2026 Adults & Health Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: Children's services forecast £3.1m overspend driven by 9% growth in residential care placement costs against 3-3.5% inflation assumed at budget-setting.
findings.detail: Children's Services overspend is £3.1m at Q1. Weekly costs for children in residential care have risen from £196k (April 2026) to £233k (June 2026), an increase of £37k per week or £1.9m annualised. Top 25 placements alone have increased from £155.5k per week to £200.9k per week (£2.36m annualised increase). Drivers include 308 children in care (highest since June 2025), with 37 new entrants May-July 2026 vs 21 same period 2025. Council notes: 'increase in complexity and higher unit costs, for placements that require a high level of supervision and care, is causing the additional pressure in demand-led services, this is often difficult to predict.'
findings.matters: Placement cost inflation running at 9% (three times assumed rate) is a core service pressure with no discretionary offset. Complexity is rising; the service cannot reduce numbers without statutory/reputational consequence. This is a multi-year pressure.
findings.figures: £3.1m Children's Services overspend; £37k per week increase in residential costs (April-June); top 25 placements up £45.4k per week (£2.36m annualised); 308 children in care
findings.quote: Between April 2026 and June 2026, total weekly costs for children in residential homes has risen from £196,000 per week to £233,000 per week (an extra £37,000 per week which equates to approximately £1.9m per year)... Increased costs are on average around 9% in the year to date

findings.committee: Culture, Community Safety & Environment Scrutiny Panel
findings.paper_title: 202627 Finance Update Report Quarter 1, 01/10/2026 Adults & Health Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: General Fund reserves of £52m are lower than average for a council of Haringey's size; General Fund Reserve of £15.1m will not be used to mitigate in-year overspend.
findings.detail: Total corporate reserves forecast £52m by March 2027, of which £28.2m is earmarked. Paper states: 'The Council's reserves position is lower than average for a council of this size and a medium to long term objective must be to increase balances to manage the many risks and uncertainties and strengthen the Council's financial resilience.' General Fund Reserve of £15.1m is being maintained 'to respond to any genuine, unforeseen pressures' and will not be drawn down to offset overspend. £23.5m corporate contingency is available but only £800k has been used at Q1.
findings.matters: A council that cannot call on its own reserves to cover overspends is financially constrained and dependent on external support (EFS). Low reserves relative to peer group leave little buffer for economic shocks, interest rate volatility, or demand surprises.
findings.figures: £52.0m total reserves forecast (March 2027); £28.2m earmarked; £15.1m General Fund Reserve; £23.5m corporate contingency available (£800k used)
findings.quote: The Council's reserves position is lower than average for a council of this size and a medium to long term objective must be to increase balances to manage the many risks and uncertainties and strengthen the Council's financial resilience... the current assumption is that this will not be used to mitigate in year overspend but be maintained to respond to any genuine, unforeseen pressures.

findings.committee: Culture, Community Safety & Environment Scrutiny Panel
findings.paper_title: 202627 Finance Update Report Quarter 1, 01/10/2026 Adults & Health Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: Capital programme underspending by £176m (24% slippage) with major schemes including regeneration and HRA acquisitions delayed.
findings.detail: Q1 forecast capital spend is £545.2m against £721.4m budget (75.6% of budget). General Fund forecast £234.4m against £344.4m budget; HRA forecast £310.7m against £376.9m budget. Major variances include: Children's £14.8m underspend (6 projects delayed through feasibility and complexity issues); Culture £46.9m underspend (Shaping Tottenham, Shaping Wood Green, High Road West slipped); HRA £66.2m underspend (acquisitions slowed, major works mobilising). Paper notes 'trend of high levels of slippage has continued into current year' and flags that schemes without business case, delivery plan and assurance will be placed into pipeline.
findings.matters: Capital slippage means either planned delivery is overoptimistic, or conditions preventing delivery are not forecast at budget-setting. Either way, a lender seeing a council underspend capital by 24% at Q1 with three-quarters of the year to run faces uncertainty on both project timeline and borrowing requirement.
findings.figures: £545.2m forecast spend against £721.4m budget; £176.2m underspend; General Fund £234.4m vs £344.4m; HRA £310.7m vs £376.9m
findings.quote: It should be noted that the trend of high levels of slippage has continued into the current year. The review of the capital programme is underway as part of the preparation for the 2027/28 capital programme that will be published in March 2027. Any scheme without an approved business case, clear delivery plan and assurance on delivery will be placed into the pipeline.

findings.committee: Culture, Community Safety & Environment Scrutiny Panel
findings.paper_title: 202627 Finance Update Report Quarter 1, 01/10/2026 Adults & Health Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecasting £3.478m deficit, driven by £10.2m income under-recovery from void properties and temporary accommodation pressures.
findings.detail: HRA is £3.5m in deficit. Main issue is £10.2m under-recovery of income from void properties, where council budgeted 2% void rate but is experiencing higher voids from decant programmes, stock turnover and acquisitions. Improvement plan in place aiming to increase void turnaround from September 2026, to be monitored through quarterly reports. Temporary accommodation within HRA contributing £2.9m overspend separately.
findings.matters: Void losses represent cash not collected that was assumed in the business plan. A landlord authority with structural void issues has working capital problems; improvement plans are often slow to deliver, and the 2% void assumption may itself be unachievable.
findings.figures: £3.478m HRA deficit forecast; £10.213m net income under-recovery from voids; 2% void rate budgeted vs higher actual
findings.quote: There is a net under recovery of income of £10.213m mainly due to a forecast higher than budgeted level of void properties throughout the year. The income profile was adjusted for a 2% void rate for 2026/27 which represents a challenging target given levels of voids that arise through decant programmes, increased stock turnover and the acquisition programme

findings.committee: Culture, Community Safety & Environment Scrutiny Panel
findings.paper_title: 202627 Finance Update Report Quarter 1, 01/10/2026 Adults & Health Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant accumulated deficit of £12.7m will remain at £3.3m even if government approves planned £9.3m SEND improvement payment.
findings.detail: DSG is forecasting £8.4m Q1 overspend, all from High Needs Block (SEND). Council has submitted SEND Improvement Plan seeking £9.4m payment which, if approved, would reduce accumulated deficit from £12.7m to £3.3m. Schools themselves in deficit: £7.7m at Q1, up from £4.1m at 2025/26 year-end. Council is working with schools on recovery plans 'which may lead to further academisation and/or closures.'
findings.matters: SEND deficits are structural (demand-led, statutory, not discretionary) and persist even with government support. Schools in deficit remain a contingent liability: council is ultimately responsible for their recovery and closure. A peer authority watching Haringey faces similar pressures.
findings.figures: £8.4m DSG overspend Q1; accumulated deficit £12.7m; potential government payment £9.4m; projected remaining deficit £3.3m; schools deficit £7.7m (Q1) up from £4.1m (year-end)
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) forecast at Quarter 1 stands at £8.4m overspend which is fully in relation to the High Needs Block... The number of schools in or facing deficits continues to rise. The 2025/26 outturn deficit for schools was £4.1m. However, at the end of quarter 1 this has increased to £7.7m.

findings.committee: Culture, Community Safety & Environment Scrutiny Panel
findings.paper_title: 202627 Finance Update Report Quarter 1, 01/10/2026 Adults & Health Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: Cross-council savings forecast only 54% delivery rate; £9.3m of target savings across two years remains unmet.
findings.detail: Cross-council savings initiatives (Commissioning, Procurement, Enabling Services, Commercial Income) total £8.7m in 2026/27, forecast 54% delivery. Of this, £5.3m also failed to deliver in 2025/26 and remains carried forward. Paper notes: 'the total target of £9.3m cashable saving must be delivered by the end of this financial year. At quarter one, this is all prudently forecast as non-deliverable.' Council expects to improve position only after due diligence by Q2.
findings.matters: Savings that fail across consecutive years cease to be credible as plans; they indicate either original overestimation, delivery failures, or both. A lender seeing a council unable to deliver its own cost-reduction programme for two years running faces elevated refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £8.7m cross-council savings target 2026/27; 54% delivery forecast (£4.65m); £5.3m carried forward from 2025/26 non-delivery; total £9.3m unmet
findings.quote: These same workstreams had £5.289m of savings in 2025/26 but did not deliver as planned last year and therefore adding to the forecast £4m 2026/27 undeliverable cross council savings, the total target of £9.3m cashable saving must be delivered by the end of this financial year. At quarter one, this is all prudently forecast as non-deliverable

findings.committee: Culture, Community Safety & Environment Scrutiny Panel
findings.paper_title: 202627 Finance Update Report Quarter 1, 01/10/2026 Adults & Health Scrutiny Panel
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support of £84.3m now forecast insufficient; council warns that borrowing to cover the gap will add £86,000 per £1m annually for 20 years.
findings.detail: Council requires £84.3m government EFS to balance the 2026/27 budget. Paper states: 'there is a substantial risk that, if the current forecast overspend on services cannot be brought down significantly and an improvement on the delivery of savings before year end, the assumed use of £84.3m of Exceptional Financial Support will not be sufficient.' Each £1m of EFS borrowed at current rates will add £86,000 annual revenue cost for 20 years at maturity.
findings.matters: EFS is already a marker of financial distress; a council anticipating it will need even more EFS signals that government support is becoming structural to the authority's finances rather than temporary, and borrowing implications compound the problem.
findings.figures: £84.3m EFS in budget; £86,000 per £1m annual cost for 20 years if borrowed
findings.quote: there is a substantial risk that, if the current forecast overspend on services cannot be brought down significantly and an improvement on the delivery of savings before year end, the assumed use of £84.3m of Exceptional Financial Support will not be sufficient. This further increases the financial burden on the authority due to increased borrowing costs. At current rates each £1m of EFS used will add £86,000 to revenue costs each year for the next 20 years

findings.headline: External borrowing increased 23.6% in one year; HRA borrowing up 17.6%
findings.detail: Total external borrowing rose from £981.3m to £1,213.4m (£232.1m increase). The underlying Capital Financing Requirement increased from £1,418.9m to £1,565.0m. HRA CFR increased particularly sharply from £626.8m to £736.9m. This trajectory, combined with high interest rates, underpins the council's assessment that borrowing growth is unsustainable.
findings.matters: A 23.6% year-on-year increase in borrowing raises sustainability questions. When a council describes its own borrowing trajectory as 'not sustainable', it signals expected financial pressure ahead.
findings.quote: the Council held £1,213.4 million in loans on 31 March 2026, an increase of £232.1 million compared to 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: PFI and finance lease liabilities breach authorised prudential limit
findings.detail: PFI and finance lease balances reached £45.0m at year-end, breaching the authorised limit of £13.9m by £31.1m and the operational boundary of £12.7m. The council explicitly notes this as an exception to full compliance. This breach was also reported at Q3.
findings.matters: Exceeding prudential limits in a specific borrowing category reduces headroom and shows the council is operating outside its approved strategy. Persistent breaches may signal deteriorating financial discipline.
findings.figures: Actual £45.0m; Authorised Limit £13.9m (breach £31.1m); Operational Boundary £12.7m.
findings.quote: all treasury management activities carried out during the period complied fully with the principles in the Treasury Management Code and the Council's approved Treasury Management Strategy with the exception of lease levels in comparison to the Operational Boundary and Authorised Limit as detailed below, which was also reported in the Quarter 3 monitoring report earlier in the year.

findings.headline: £50m LOBO loans face refinancing demand within 12 months at materially higher rates
findings.detail: All £50m of Haringey's LOBO loans have call dates within April 2026. If lenders exercise these options, the council will need to refinance or repay. Current market rates for 10-year PWLB borrowing (5.72%) are substantially higher than the LOBO loans' current 4.73% rate.
findings.matters: This is an immediate refinancing obligation. If lenders call, the council faces significantly higher borrowing costs when refinancing at current rates, increasing annual debt service.
findings.figures: £50m LOBO loans at 4.73% weighted average rate. Next call dates: 10/04/2026. Current 10-year PWLB rate: 5.72%.
findings.quote: All LOBO loans the Council held at year end have call dates within the next 12 months.

findings.headline: Council reviewing capital programme to identify schemes that can be paused or slowed; external borrowing increased £232.1m to £1,213.4m
findings.detail: Haringey will review its capital programme during summer 2026 to identify schemes that can be paused or slowed. The council explicitly cites high interest rates, ongoing reliance on EFS, and unsustainable year-on-year borrowing increases as drivers. This represents a material shift in capital spending plans.
findings.matters: A council actively pausing capital schemes signals financial distress and indicates a deterioration in financial position. For lenders, this is a leading indicator of financial difficulty and reduced investment capacity.
findings.figures: External borrowing increased £232.1m to £1,213.4m in 2025/26. Capital Financing Requirement increased £146.1m to £1,565.0m.
findings.quote: the Council will be reviewing its capital programme to identify schemes that can be paused  / slowed down given that interest rates remain high , reliance on EFS remains high and forecast year on year increase on borrowing is not sustainable.

findings.headline: Council seeks to reduce reliance on Exceptional Financial Support through increased savings delivery
findings.detail: The statutory officer's finance comments note that acceptance of KPMG's recommendations and council actions is 'expected to increase the level of savings agreed by the Council for 2027/28 onwards, improve delivery of these savings and reduce future reliance on Exceptional Financial Support.' This indicates the council currently depends on emergency government funding to balance its budget.
findings.matters: Councils reliant on Exceptional Financial Support are in financial distress; reducing that reliance requires closing structural deficits through service cuts or transformation, which poses ongoing financial risk.
findings.figures: None specific on savings gaps or EFS amounts
findings.quote: The Statutory Recommendation and Non-Statutory Recommendations and the actions by the Council is expected to increase the level of savings agreed by the Council for 2027/28 onwards, improve delivery of these savings and reduce future reliance on Exceptional Financial Support

findings.matters: Creation of a high-level recovery board with chief-executive-level oversight and monthly monitoring suggests the council acknowledges significant financial management weakness and is implementing additional governance controls over savings delivery.

findings.headline: External auditor issues Statutory Recommendation due to inadequate planned savings in 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: KPMG warned in its January 2026 annual report that it would issue a Statutory Recommendation if the 2026/27 budget lacked adequate planned savings to address the council's 'challenging financial position'. When the council approved the 2026/27 budget on 2 March 2026, KPMG issued the Statutory Recommendation on 18 May 2026.
findings.matters: Statutory Recommendations from external auditors are rare formal escalations indicating the auditor believes the council's financial sustainability is threatened; this signals serious budget-balancing problems to lenders and regulators.

findings.detail: Auditors note unresolved data quality issues: 'Given known issues in the prior year with the reliability of information regarding Beacon properties which prevented our conclusion over Council Dwellings in 24/25, we will have a specific focus on this area during the audit.' findings.headline: Adult Social Care has CQC 'Requires Improvement' finding and council lacks adequate financial forecasting and management of this spend
findings.detail: Auditors have identified a significant VFM risk: the council lacks adequate processes to forecast and manage Adult Social Care spend in light of the CQC's 'Requires Improvement' rating. There are also concerns about timely assessment and recovery of patient contributions.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is typically the largest council budget. A CQC 'Requires Improvement' finding signals service stress. Combined with poor forecasting controls, this creates material risk of budget overruns and demand-driven overspends.
findings.figures: CQC rating: Requires Improvement
findings.quote: the Council does not have adequate processes in place to ensure that Social Care spend is sufficiently forecast and managed in light of the 'Requires Improvement' CQC findings, or that financial contributions from patients are assessed and recovered in a timely manner.

findings.headline: Council's budget shortfall is escalating: £54m Exceptional Financial Support in 2025/26, but already forecasting £84m need for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council faced a forecasted overspend of £19m at Q3 2025/26, improved to £14m by Month 11. It received an additional £17m EFS in February 2026 (bringing total to £54m) to meet the shortfall. It is already forecasting it will require £84m EFS for 2026/27 to balance its budget.
findings.matters: EFS is non-recurring government support. The escalation from £54m to £84m shows the council's underlying budget position is worsening significantly, not improving. This raises questions about long-term financial sustainability and the ability to service debt.
findings.figures: £54m EFS in 2025/26, £84m EFS required for 2026/27; £19m Q3 overspend, reduced to £14m by Month 11
findings.quote: Furthermore, the Council has faced difficulties in delivering this budget, with a forecasted overspend of £19m as at Q3, subsequently improved to £14m as at Month 11... MHCLG has approved an additional Exceptional Finance Support (EFS) allocation of £17m (to £54m) to the Council in February 2026 to meet the budget shortfall... The Council is also forecasting a substantial budget shortfall for 26/27 which required an agreed £84m EFS allocation in 26/27 with MHCLG to reach a balanced position.

findings.headline: Council has had disclaimed audit opinions for three consecutive years (2022/23–2024/25) and is undergoing rebuilding assurance work to restore audit opinion
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimer of opinion from the predecessor auditor for three years through 2022/23, a disclaimer for 2023/24 issued on 28 February 2025, and a disclaimed opinion for 2024/25 issued on 26 February 2026. The auditors are now conducting a formal rebuilding assurance risk assessment as part of the national 'Rest and Recovery' programme.
findings.matters: Three consecutive years of disclaimed opinions signals the council has struggled to produce auditable financial statements. This is a fundamental issue for lenders assessing financial reliability and governance.
findings.figures: 3 consecutive years of disclaimed opinions
findings.quote: For Haringey London Borough Council, this had the impact of a disclaimer of opinion issued by your predecessor auditor for 3 financial years up to and including 2022/23. We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 28 February 2025 to comply with the statutory backstop date as reported to you previously. For the 2024/25 audit we issued a disclaimed opinion on 26 February 2026.

findings.headline: Real-terms funding cuts of £143m since 2010; ~80% of budget locked into mandatory services
findings.detail: Haringey has experienced cumulative real-terms funding reductions of £143m over 16 years. Around 80% of the budget is committed to services the council is legally required to deliver (social care, temporary accommodation, education). This leaves minimal discretionary spending and makes it nearly impossible to balance budgets through service reductions alone.
findings.matters: The structural funding gap, combined with fixed mandatory spending, means the council cannot simply cut its way to balance. This supports the auditors' assessment that savings targets are unachievable without transformational change, and suggests 2026/27 budget approval without adequate planned savings (which triggered the statutory recommendation) was unrealistic.
findings.figures: £143m real-terms cut since 2010, 80% budget spent on mandatory services
findings.quote: Since the onset of austerity in 2010, real terms funding in Haringey has been cut by £143 million... around 80% of our budget being spent on services we must deliver.
